summary: Extends the Remote Network Monitoring MIB with objects for watching IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A network probe is a device that watches a network and collects statistics about it, which an SNMP manager then reads over the network. This RFC adds the counters and tables a probe needs when the network it watches is Token Ring, including how each station on the ring is behaving and in what order the stations sit.

what is the rmon token ring mib
subtitle: The extra counters a network probe needs to watch an IEEE 802.5 Token Ring.

tldr.problem: The Remote Network Monitoring MIB defined the objects a probe collects, but the statistics and history groups described the data link layer in Ethernet terms, so a Token Ring network could not be monitored with them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines Token Ring versions of the statistics and history groups, and adds four groups that make no sense on Ethernet: the ring station group, the ring station order group, the ring station configuration group and the source routing statistics group.
tldr.outcome: The memo was a standards-track specification that updated the RMON MIB, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it.

today: RFC 1513 is a September 1993 standards-track memo that updated the RMON MIB, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the Token Ring additions to the monitoring MIB.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework has three components. STD 16, RFC 1155, defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management, and STD 16, RFC 1212, defines a more concise description mechanism that is wholly consistent with the SMI. STD 17, RFC 1213, defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, and STD 15, RFC 1157, defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, or MIB. Within a given MIB module, objects are defined using the OBJECT-TYPE macro of RFC 1212, and at a minimum each object has a name, a syntax, an access level and an implementation status.

The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name specifying an object type. The object type together with an object instance identifies a specific instantiation of the object, and for human convenience a textual string, the object descriptor, is often used as well. The syntax of an object type defines the abstract data structure corresponding to that object type, and ASN.1 is used for this purpose, though RFC 1155 deliberately restricts the ASN.1 constructs that may be used, explicitly for simplicity. The access level says whether it makes protocol sense to read or write the value of an instance of the object type, and is independent of any administrative authorization policy. The implementation status says whether the object is mandatory, optional, obsolete or deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP lets a manager read counters from a device. The counters and other values are described in a MIB, where each one has a name, a type, a rule about who may read or write it, and a status saying whether an implementation must provide it.

sections.title: Implementing the RFC 1271 Objects on Token Ring
sections.content:
Wherever a MacAddress is used in this MIB, the source routing bit is stripped off, so that the resulting address is consistently valid for all packets sent by a particular node.

In the Host Group, only Token Ring isolating errors increment the error counter for a particular host entry. The isolating errors are LineErrors, BurstErrors, ACErrors, InternalErrors and AbortErrors. ACErrors increment the error counter only for the nearest upstream neighbour of the station reporting the error. LineErrors and BurstErrors increment the error counters for the station reporting the error and for its upstream neighbour. InternalErrors and AbortErrors increment the error counter for the station reporting the error only. Congestion errors are also counted for each host entry, and all of these errors are incremented in the host entry of the station that reports them in an error report frame. The hostOutPkts and hostOutOctets counters are not incremented for packets with errors.

In the Matrix Group, error counters are never incremented. In the Filter Group, the status bitmask for Token Ring networks is made up of bit 3, first packet after some packets were dropped, bit 4, packet with the Frame Copied Bit set, and bit 5, packet with the Address Recognized Bit set. For the packet match algorithm, the filters assume a 32 byte RIF field, so the filter is compared to the packet starting at the AC byte until the end of the RIF field, and the unused RIF bytes in the filter are then skipped. Any filter care bits in the RIF that do not correspond to bytes in the input packet cause the filter to fail.

Because soft error report packets may be sent with assured delivery, some errors may accidentally be reported twice on devices that perform the RMON function promiscuously.
sections.plainLanguage: Token Ring reports errors differently from Ethernet, so the RFC spells out which error counts against which station. It also explains that a filter on a Token Ring packet has to match the route information field, and that a promiscuous probe may count the same soft error twice.

sections.title: The MIB Groups Added for Token Ring
sections.content:
The Remote Network Monitoring MIB, RFC 1271, defines a framework for remote monitoring functions implemented on a network probe, and breaks its objects down into nine functional groups. Some of those groups, the statistics and the history groups, have a view of the data link layer that is specific to the media type and require specific objects to be defined for each media type. RFC 1271 defined the specific objects necessary for Ethernet, and this memo defines those specific objects necessary for Token Ring LANs. In addition, it defines monitoring functions that are specific to Token Ring.

The Token Ring statistics groups contain current utilization and error statistics, and are broken into the Token Ring Mac-Layer Statistics Group, which collects information from the MAC layer including error reports for the ring and ring utilization, and the Token Ring Promiscuous Statistics Group, which collects utilization statistics from data packets collected promiscuously. The Token Ring history groups have the same shape but hold historical statistics, in the Token Ring Mac-Layer History Group and the Token Ring Promiscuous History Group.

The Token Ring Ring Station Group contains statistics and status information associated with each Token Ring station on the local ring, and also provides status information for each ring being monitored. The Token Ring Ring Station Order Group provides the order of the stations on monitored rings. The Token Ring Ring Station Config Group manages Token Ring stations through active means, so any station on a monitored ring may be removed or have configuration information downloaded from it. The Token Ring Source Routing Group contains utilization statistics derived from the source routing information optionally present in Token Ring packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The probe's MIB grows by four groups that only make sense on a ring, plus Token Ring versions of the general statistics and history tables. The new groups report on each station, on the order of the stations around the ring, on station configuration, and on how much traffic the ring's source routing is carrying.

sections.title: The Mac-Layer Statistics Entry
sections.content:
The Token Ring Mac-Layer Statistics Group is a table of statistics entries, each kept for a particular Token Ring interface, and each entry is indexed by an integer between 1 and 65535. A second object identifies the source of the data, which can be any Token Ring interface on the device, identified by the instance of the ifIndex object from MIB-II. The statistics in the group reflect all error reports on the local network segment attached to the identified interface, and that object may not be modified while the entry status is valid.

The entry collects a set of counters. The traffic counters are dropEvents, the number of times the probe lacked resources to handle a packet, macOctets, the total octets of data in good frames received, and macPkts, the number of good frames received. The ring state counters are ringPurgeEvents, the number of times the ring enters the ring purge state from the normal ring state, ringPurgePkts, beaconEvents, the number of times the ring enters a beaconing state from a non-beaconing state, beaconTime, the total time the ring has been beaconing, beaconPkts, claimTokenEvents, claimTokenPkts, and NAUNChanges. The error counters are lineErrors, internalErrors, burstErrors, ACErrors, abortErrors, lostFrameErrors, congestionErrors, frameCopiedErrors, frequencyErrors, tokenErrors and softErrorReports, together with a ringPollEvents counter.

Each counter is marked mandatory, and the table itself is mandatory, although the implementation of the group is optional. The entry also carries an owner string and a status object.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the main statistics table. For each Token Ring interface the probe watches, it keeps counters for traffic, for ring state such as beaconing and purging, and for each kind of error the ring can report, and the same counters are also kept over time in the history group.

sections.title: The Ring Station Tables
sections.content:
The Ring Station Group has a control table, with one entry for each ring being monitored, and a station table, with an entry for each station that is now or has previously been detected as physically present on a ring. A station entry is indexed by the interface on which the station was detected and by its MAC address, and it holds the physical address of the last known NAUN of the station, the times it last entered and last exited the ring taken from sysUpTime, and counters for duplicate addresses and for line, burst, internal, abort, lost frame, congestion, frame copied, frequency and token errors, in and out beacon errors, and insertions.

The status of a station is one of three values: active, meaning it is actively participating in the ring poll; inactive, meaning it is not participating in the ring poll; and forcedRemoval, meaning it was forced off the ring by network management. The control entry for a ring carries the address of the Active Monitor on the segment, which is six octets of zero if unknown, and a count of the add and delete events in the ring station order table.

The Ring Station Order Group holds the order of the stations on monitored rings, indexed by the interface and by an order index, with the MAC address of the station at that position. The Ring Station Config Group manages stations actively: entries exist in its table after an active configuration query has completed successfully for a station, and each entry holds the update time, the assigned physical location of the station, its microcode, its group address and its functional address.

The Source Routing Group counts frames and octets that came into the ring from another ring, that left the ring for another ring, that passed through it from one ring to another, and the good frames received that were All Routes Broadcast or Single Route Broadcast.
sections.plainLanguage: These tables let a manager see each machine on the ring, when it joined and left, which errors it reported, where it sits in the ring order, and what its configured address and location are. A manager can also read a station's configuration or take it off the ring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states plainly that security issues are not discussed in it. What it does say about access sits in the framework section: the access level of an object type defines whether it makes protocol sense to read or write the value of an instance of that object type, and the RFC notes that this access level is independent of any administrative authorization policy. So the tables in this MIB describe what may be read or changed, and the question of who is allowed to do so is settled elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about security. It does say that an object's access level is about protocol sense, not about who is allowed to read it, so authorization has to be handled by the system running the agent.

viz.caption: THE MIB GROUPS THIS RFC ADDS FOR TOKEN RING

items.title: Mac-Layer Statistics
items.text: Current utilization and error statistics taken from the MAC layer.

items.title: Promiscuous Statistics
items.text: Utilization statistics from data packets collected promiscuously.

items.title: Mac-Layer History
items.text: The same MAC layer figures, kept over time.

items.title: Promiscuous History
items.text: The same promiscuous figures, kept over time.

items.title: Ring Station
items.text: Statistics and status for each station on the local ring, and for the ring itself.

items.title: Ring Station Order
items.text: The order of the stations around a monitored ring.

items.title: Ring Station Config
items.text: Active management of stations, including downloading configuration.

items.title: Source Routing
items.text: Utilization statistics from the source routing information in Token Ring packets.
